narrative:
The model estimates a 79.0% chance that you will leave your job. Under the promotion rule, that high leave risk is why you are being denied a promotion: the decision is not a judgment of your worth, but a forecast that you may not remain with the organization long enough to justify advancement.

The strongest signal pushing toward leaving is that you report other job opportunities. This is uncommon among employees predicted to stay—only about 23% have other opportunities—so it strongly raises concern that you may move. Second is your total experience of 6–10 years. Employees predicted to stay are more often in the 1–5 year range (50.4%), so your longer overall experience adds to the leaving signal. Third is your 1–5 years with your current organization. Although this tenure is common among stayers (51.2%), in your combination of factors it still pushes the forecast toward leaving rather than staying.

For next steps, the organization should discuss retention openly: your career path, promotion timing, and how your current role compares with outside options. You should clarify your intentions and what would make you stay, while also weighing those external opportunities and any work-life or recognition concerns. A retention conversation and a concrete development plan are more useful now than treating the promotion denial as final.
